original_question: Prove that a simple(that is, without proper non-trivial connected normal subgroups) algebraic group M over an algebraically closed field cannot act definably, faithfully, and irreducibly on a simple group of finite Morley rank other than M/Z(M).
target_in_paper: Problem 21.21 in the section "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)"
correct_elements: Your draft is extremely close to the paper's official formulation and in substance matches Problem 21.21 almost verbatim. It correctly identifies the acting group M as a simple algebraic group over an algebraically closed field, uses the paper's parenthetical meaning of simplicity for M, places the target in the class of simple groups of finite Morley rank, and keeps exactly the three action hypotheses used in the problem: definable, faithful, and irreducible. It also preserves the same exceptional case M/Z(M).
missing_details: To make the question fully stand-alone, the paper's nearby definition of an irreducible action should be spelled out: M leaves invariant no definable non-trivial proper subgroup of the target group S.
For complete self-containment, Z(M) should be identified as the center of M.
If one wants the action hypothesis fully explicit, one should say that the action map M x S -> S is definable and that faithfulness means the kernel is trivial.
The phrase "other than M/Z(M)" is best unpacked as: if such an action exists on a simple group S of finite Morley rank, then necessarily S is isomorphic to M/Z(M).
refined_question: Let M be a simple algebraic group over an algebraically closed field, where "simple" means that M has no proper non-trivial connected normal subgroups, and let Z(M) denote the center of M. Suppose that M acts on a simple group S of finite Morley rank by a definable action M x S -> S with trivial kernel, and assume that the action is irreducible in the sense that M preserves no definable non-trivial proper subgroup of S. Must it follow that S is isomorphic to M/Z(M)?
justification: The draft clearly targets Problem 21.21, whose wording it reproduces almost exactly. The only nearby hidden definition needed to make it stand-alone is the meaning of "irreducible," supplied immediately before in Problem 21.19 on the same page. Problem 21.20 shows the immediate local context: Borovik is posing a short sequence of questions excluding faithful definable irreducible actions on simple groups of finite Morley rank except for the obvious self-type case.
